content: Preterm birth is a significant health issue, accounting for over 50% of perinatal mortality. It is associated with various risk factors, such as cervical incompetence and multiple pregnancies. To address this, several management strategies have been explored, including cervical cerclage. However, cervical cerclage is an invasive procedure requiring anesthesia and carries potential complications. Additionally, there is ongoing debate about its effectiveness and the specific patient groups that may benefit from it. Cervical pessary has emerged as a simpler, non-invasive alternative to cervical cerclage for preventing preterm birth. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy of cervical pessary in preventing preterm birth among women at risk due to cervical incompetence. A systematic search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, Current Controlled Trials, and the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, with the last search performed on September 1, 2012. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized clinical trials comparing cervical pessary with cervical cerclage or expectant management. Quasi-randomized, cluster-randomized, or cross-over trials were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion. The review included one randomized controlled trial involving 385 pregnant women with a cervical length of 25 mm or less, between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation. Among these, 192 women received a cervical pessary, while the rest underwent expectant management. The use of a cervical pessary significantly reduced the incidence of spontaneous preterm birth before 37 weeks of gestation compared to expectant management (22% vs. 59%; risk ratio [RR] 0.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.27 to 0.49). Similarly, spontaneous preterm birth before 34 weeks was also significantly lower in the pessary group (6% vs. 27%; RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.43). The mean gestational age at delivery was higher in the pessary group (37.7 ± 2 weeks) compared to the expectant group (34.9 ± 4 weeks). Women in the pessary group required fewer tocolytics (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.81) and corticosteroids (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.81) than those in the expectant group. However, vaginal discharge was more frequently reported in the pessary group (RR 2.18, 95% CI 1.87 to 2.54). Among the pessary group, 27 women required repositioning of the pessary without removal, and one woman had the pessary removed. Notably, 95% of women in the pessary group stated they would recommend this intervention to others. Neonatal admission to pediatric care was significantly reduced in the pessary group compared to the expectant group (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.42). In conclusion, this review included a single well-designed randomized clinical trial, which demonstrated that cervical pessary is effective in reducing preterm birth in women with a short cervix. However, further trials are necessary to evaluate its efficacy in different populations, including those in developed and developing countries, and among women with other risk factors, such as multiple pregnancies.
